heard: This man sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap metal. Paris, 1925. Victor Lustig is reading the paper when he spots a tiny story. The tower is rusting and repainting it costs a fortune. So, he forges government letterhead and becomes a deputy director at the Ministry of Posts. He books a suite at the Hotel de Crayons and invites five scrap dealers. His pitch? The city is secretly tearing the tower down. Seven thousand tons of iron. One dealer, André Poisson, wants it badly. But something feels off. So, Lustig makes a confession. He's a corrupt official, and he needs a bribe. You see, to Poisson, the bribe was the proof. Only a real official would ask for one. So, Poisson pays $20,000 plus $50,000 more to win. Within the hour, Lustig is on a train to Vienna with the cash. He waits for the headlines. Nothing. Poisson is too embarrassed to report it. So, Lustig comes back to Paris and tries to sell the tower again. This time, the buyer calls the police, and Lustig escapes to America. But historians have never found a single police report. The only proof might be a con man's word.
